lines.text:
Watching the Universe — A Night at the Observatory

An observatory is built for one purpose: to see what the unaided eye cannot. Positioned on mountaintops far from city light, these facilities house the instruments that have revealed the structure of the cosmos — from the planets of our solar system to galaxies billions of light-years away.

The centrepiece is the telescope. An optical telescope gathers visible light. A reflecting telescope uses a curved mirror to focus starlight. A refracting telescope uses a lens. A radio telescope — a large dish or array of dishes — detects radio waves emitted by distant objects. Each telescope sits on a telescope mount that tracks objects as the Earth rotates, compensating for the planet's rotation so that a star remains centred in the eyepiece. A finder scope — a small auxiliary telescope — helps locate targets before the main instrument magnifies them.

The dome is the observatory's most recognisable feature. A rotating roof opens a slit to the sky, allowing the telescope to point at any part of the visible hemisphere. The observation deck — the platform where astronomers work — surrounds the telescope base. A control room houses the computers that operate the telescope remotely. A computer lab processes the enormous volumes of data each night produces. A library stores decades of published research. A lecture hall hosts public talks and academic seminars. A gift shop sells star charts and educational materials. A pathway connects the buildings, lit by red flashlights — red light preserves night vision while white light destroys it.

Modern astronomy is largely digital. A CCD camera — a highly sensitive electronic sensor — has replaced the photographic plate. A spectrograph breaks light into its component wavelengths, revealing a star's temperature, composition, and velocity. A photometer measures brightness with extreme precision. A data server stores terabytes of observations. A computer monitor displays real-time images. A laser pointer identifies objects during public viewing sessions.

The objects astronomers study span every scale. A star is a self-luminous sphere of gas. A planet orbits a star. A moon orbits a planet — our Moon is the closest celestial body. The Sun is our nearest star. A comet — ice and dust trailing a glowing tail — visits the inner solar system on an elongated orbit. An asteroid is a rocky body, most found in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. A meteor — a streak of light — is a small particle burning in Earth's atmosphere. A nebula is a cloud of gas where new stars form. A galaxy contains billions of stars. A constellation is a pattern of stars as seen from Earth — not a physical grouping but a line-of-sight arrangement.

The planets of our solar system — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and the dwarf planet Pluto — are among the first objects students learn to find. Each has a magnitude — a measure of brightness — and an orbit measured in Earth years.

Observatory activities include star gazing, astrophotography, data analysis, public viewing nights, night tours, lectures, research, sky mapping, eclipse watching, and meteor shower observation. An eclipse — the alignment of Sun, Moon, and Earth — is among the most dramatic events. A transit occurs when a smaller body crosses the face of a larger one.

Every spectrum analysed, every orbit calculated, every discovery published adds a line to humanity's longest-running project: understanding where we are in the universe and what surrounds us in the dark.

lines.text: 'Astronomy' = the scientific study of stars, planets, and the universe. 'Astrology' = the belief that stars and planets influence human lives (horoscopes). They are completely different! An 'astronomer' is a scientist; an 'astrologer' reads horoscopes. Never confuse them.

Hubble Space Telescope — orbiting telescope launched in 1990 that revolutionized our understanding of the universe.

lines.text: A 'light year' is a unit of distance, not time. It's the distance light travels in one year — about 9.46 trillion kilometres. Common mistake: 'That happened light years ago' — this sounds natural in casual English but is technically mixing distance and time. Scientists measure distances in light years, parsecs, or astronomical units (AU).

lines.text: 'Constellation' = a group of stars forming a pattern (e.g. Orion, the Great Bear). 'Nebula' = a cloud of gas and dust in space. 'Galaxy' = a system of millions of stars (our galaxy is the Milky Way). 'Comet' = an icy body with a tail that orbits the Sun. 'Meteor' = a shooting star. 'Meteorite' = a meteor that reaches Earth's surface.

lines.text: 'Discovery' is the noun; 'discover' is the verb. Common noun–verb pairs: discover/discovery, decide/decision, arrive/arrival, choose/choice, succeed/success. At B2, distinguish: 'They made a discovery' (noun) vs. 'They discovered a new comet' (verb). Similar trap: 'an important research' — 'research' is uncountable (use 'a piece of research' or 'a research finding').

lines.text: Never combine 'most' with '-est.' Short adjectives: add '-est': 'largest', 'brightest', 'nearest.' Long adjectives: use 'most': 'most spectacular', 'most distant.' Irregular: 'good → best', 'bad → worst', 'far → farthest/furthest.' 'More' and '-er' follow the same mutual exclusion rule: 'bigger' not *'more bigger.'

lines.text: Present perfect continuous: have/has + been + -ing: 'have been studying.' The continuous emphasises duration and ongoing activity. 'Have studied' (present perfect simple) emphasises completion or result. 'Have been studying' (continuous) emphasises the process still in progress. Never *'have been studied' for continuous — that's passive: 'The star has been studied by many teams.'

lines.text: 'Fewer' + countable plural: 'fewer stars', 'fewer planets', 'fewer observations.' 'Less' + uncountable: 'less light', 'less cloud cover', 'less interference.' Common error: using 'less' with countable nouns. Exception in informal speech: 'less than ten items' is widely accepted, but in formal/academic writing, 'fewer than ten' is preferred.
